pronunciation.approximation: or-FEWS — the stress lands on the last syllable.
pronunciation.note: Greek Ὀρφεύς stresses the final syllable — Orpheús — and the restoration keeps the acute where the tradition puts it. The etymology is debated (perhaps from a root for 'orphan' or the 'darkness' of his descent); the name is older than its explanations, which is exactly right for the singer who is all voice.

domains.title: The Singer of the World
domains.subtitle: Music, Poetry, the Descent, and the Lost Look Back
domains.lead: Orpheús is the archetype of art itself: the Thracian singer whose lyre moved stones and stopped rivers, who went down living into the underworld for his wife, and whose single look back is the West's permanent parable of love and loss.

cards.name: The Lyre
cards.desc: His instrument: the gift of Apóllōn, the sound that made nature stop to listen.

cards.name: The Argonauts
cards.desc: His song steadied the Argo's crew past the Seirḗnes — art as navigation.

cards.name: The Descent
cards.desc: The katabasis for Eurydikē — the only route out of death that music ever opened.

cards.name: The Look Back
cards.desc: The one forbidden glance, at the threshold — and the second, final loss.

symbols.name: The lyre
symbols.meaning: Art as the measure of the world — the cosmos tuned to a string.

symbols.name: The laurel
symbols.meaning: The crown of his prophetic grove at Pieria, where trees learned to move.

symbols.name: The nightingale
symbols.meaning: Song persisting through darkness — the bird of his native Thrace.

symbols.name: The river Hebrus
symbols.meaning: The stream that carried his still-singing head down to the sea and ashore at Lesbos.

symbols.name: The constellation Lyra
symbols.meaning: His lyre set among the stars — the only instrument in the sky.

mythology.lead: Orpheús' myths are all about what music can and cannot do: it charms everything in nature, opens the underworld's doors, and saves nothing except itself. Epic, lyric, and Roman poetry, and finally the mystery-religion that took his name, turn one Thracian singer into the West's permanent anatomy of art, love, and loss.

myths.title: The Song that Moves Stones
myths.text: Genealogy made him art's aristocrat — son of Kalliopē, Muse of epic, by the Thracian king Oeagrus; or, in the version that flatters him more, by Apóllōn himself (Apollodorus 1.3.2). What he did with the inheritance became proverbial. When Orpheús played, the tradition insists, nature suspended its habits: trees unrooted and followed him down from Pieria, rivers halted mid-course, wild beasts lay down with sheep, and the oldest surviving witness, a line of Simonides (fr. 567 PMG), has 'the birds flying above him, the fishes leaping from the blue deep' — repeated almost verbatim by Apollonius Rhodius (Argonautica 1.23–34). The exaggeration is the point. No one claims Orpheús won a war; his was the one power the gods could not do better — harmony, which is to say the world persuaded rather than forced. Greek art never wrote a stronger claim for itself: song is not entertainment but government, over a jurisdiction that includes the stones.

myths.title: The Singer on the Argo
myths.text: Apollonius Rhodius gives the hero's gift its most practical use. On the Argo, Orpheús is not decoration: his lyre sets the rowers' time and stills the quarrels of heroes crowded on one deck (Argonautica 1.494–515, 1.540–546), and — at the passage of the Seirḗnes — his song saves the expedition outright, drowning the death-song in a nobler strain until the lethal shore is past (Argonautica 4.885–919). Pindar had already numbered him among the Argonauts (Pythian 4.176 ff.) as the one indispensable passenger who carried no weapon. The episode is the epic's quiet thesis: the most dangerous stretch of the most dangerous voyage in Greek legend is survived not by a blade but by a string, tuned. Every crew since — rowing, sailing, singing at the oars — has unknowingly rehearsed his passage, and every navy that still pipes its rowers keeps his discipline without his name.

myths.title: The Look Back
myths.text: Eurydíkē died of a viper's bite on their wedding day, and Orpheús answered with the act that defines him: he went down after her, alive. Katabasis was Odysseus' desperate errand and Herakles' labor; Orpheús went by the invitation of his own gift. His song stilled Charon's oar, silenced the triple throat of Cerberus, and stopped the whips of the Erinyes mid-stroke; the shades wept, and Hádēs himself relented — on one condition: she would follow behind him, and he must not turn to look until both stood in the upper light. The poets differ on the fatal instant — Virgil makes him 'conquered in mind' (Georgics 4.491), Ovid blames the forgetfulness of desperate love (Metamorphoses 10.56–57) — but all agree on the geography of the loss: the threshold. He looked. She fell back, already his, saying only 'farewell.' The West has been writing the sentence ever since: love almost defeats death — almost — and the whole distance between the two words is one glance.

myths.title: The Head that Sang
myths.text: The end matches the gift in strangeness. In Ovid's telling (Metamorphoses 10.78–11.66), Orpheús withdrew from all love after losing Eurydíkē — and the Thracian women, Maenads of Dionysos or jilted brides, the versions disagree, tore him apart on the banks of the Hebrus in a Bacchic frenzy. Even dismembered he kept singing: the head floated down the river, still calling 'Eurydíkē,' out into the sea and ashore at Lesbos, where for ages it prophesied from a cave until Apóllōn silenced it; and the lyre, set in the sky, became the constellation Lyra (Ovid, Metamorphoses 11.1–66). The Orphics, whose own god died in pieces, found their patron in him — a singer who preaches the soul's journey and is himself the journey's price. The myth's last mercy is exact: the song survives the singer, and what killed him is precisely what he would not stop doing.

lore.syncretism: The mystery-religion that took his name — Orphism — made him the patron of the soul's journey: the gold tablets, the cosmic egg, Phánēs, and the map of the afterlife all carry the Orphic brand, though the historical singer and the theology are centuries apart. Christianity read him as a type of Christ — the descent, the harrowing, the charming of the animals — and he appears in that role in early Christian art. The Renaissance made him the emblem of poetry itself, the divine Orpheus who tunes the world's discord into concord. And opera was effectively invented for him: Monteverdi's Orfeo (1607) is the first great opera, and the hundreds that followed — from Gluck to Offenbach — keep re-judging the look back, which is to say they keep re-trying the threshold.
lore.culturalLegacy: 'Orphic' is the word for haunting, entrancing beauty; the lyre constellation (Lyra) is his; and the look-back is literature's most quoted failure — from Virgil to Rilke's Sonnets to Orpheus to Cocteau's Orphée and on through film and musical after film and musical. Every artist who has tried to retrieve something from loss — and failed at the threshold of the work — is his descendant. Music's power to move the world is his biography; its limits are his lesson. Few figures who may never have lived have been so thoroughly employed: the West has used him, for twenty-five centuries, as its permanent rehearsal of the one question art cannot answer — whether the song was worth the wife.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Orpheús is the patron of the almost. He retrieved her — almost. He sang the Erinyes to stillness — and still lost. His question is the one every artist and every lover knows: when the rule is 'do not look back,' and the one thing you possess is the looking, what are you willing to lose for a single glimpse of what you love?

The tradition has never decided whether the look was a failure or the final proof of love — Virgil convicts him, Ovid pities him, Rilke forgives him, because without the look there would be no song. Perhaps that is the myth's deepest economy: the loss of Eurydíkē is the price of everything Orphic that followed — the mysteries, the tablets, the poems, and the whole long culture of singing against the dark. The lyre, not the wife, reached the stars; and every artist since has suspected the trade was, somehow, the only one available.
lore.archaeology: The Orphic gold tablets — thin gold leaves buried with initiates from Thessaly to South Italy, instructing the dead ('say: I am a child of Earth and starry Heaven') — are his cult's material archive. Vase-painting shows him in Thracian dress charming the Greeks, then charming the animals, then (a favorite Roman motif) playing to underworld figures; the Piraeus relief of Orpheús charming the animals (Piraeus Museum) and the singer-cult sites at Pangaion mark his geography. On Lesbos, the ancient tradition placed his head's landing at Antissa, where the oracle of the head was remembered into late antiquity.
